column1: “You people are paid to say this.”
column2: I'm with the campaign, and I won't pretend otherwise. That's why I'd rather give you facts you can check yourself than slogans. If anything I say is wrong, tell me and I'll follow up.
column3: Honesty about who you are builds trust. Never deny being with the campaign.

column2: Let them finish. Then: "You sound really frustrated, and you have every right to be. Can you tell me what's hit you hardest?" Listen, pick their one main issue, and answer only that.
column3: Never argue back or raise your voice. If abuse continues, thank them politely and end the call.

column1: What is the golden rule for every caller response?
column2: Acknowledge the voter's concern first, then give one sourced fact. Never dispute what a voter has lived through.
column3: Aim for replies of about 15 seconds; use the backup only if the voter pushes back.

column1: What should a caller do when asked for a figure they don't have?
column2: Offer to follow up with the verified number. Never guess.

column1: How should a caller end a call politely?
column2: Thank the voter for their time, repeat one point they cared about, and invite them to check their name on the voter register (final register due 15 December 2026).
column3: End warmly even if they disagree: today's "no" can become a "maybe".

column2: Claims voters can disprove from their own lives ("electricity is fixed", "kidnapping is over", "food is cheap now") destroy trust. Honest acknowledgement plus verified delivery persuades more.
